title: Can’t Need It, Gotta Want It
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: In a short, pointed essay on teacher identity, Stuart argues that teachers cannot afford to need recognition of any kind, from the grateful former student in the supermarket to the award or the book deal. Needing affirmation, he contends, is a popular but avoidable minefield: it surrenders a teacher's autonomy to external scorecards and leaves him reduced to ashes the moment a student says he hates the class. He anticipates the objection that the only alternative is apathy and inverts it, claiming that the affirmation-seeker actually cares less, because the affirmation is about the teacher and not the students. His sharpest line is that many teachers confuse loving their students with loving how their students make them feel. He prescribes three steps: admit an 'external locus of identity', do the internal work of shedding it, and redirect the drive toward wanting results for the students. Detaching self-worth from the work, he concludes, is not caring less but the precondition of caring cleanly and teaching courageously.
points: Stuart's core distinction is between needing affirmation and wanting results; the first enslaves a teacher to externals, the second directs energy to students' actual flourishing.
He claims the need for recognition sets teachers up to be demolished by its opposite, since a single student's contempt becomes devastating to anyone who depends on student approval.
His most pointed diagnosis is that many teachers who believe they love their students actually love the way their students make them feel.
He anticipates and rejects the charge that detachment breeds apathy, arguing that separating self-worth from the job is the only way to care about students cleanly.
The remedy is framed as a three-step internal discipline: recognize an external locus of identity, take it off, and replace it with a drive for students' long-term results.
quotes: My message today is simple. We cannot afford to need this kind of recognition, or any kind of recognition.

Too many teachers needlessly brutalize themselves by needing recognition or affirmation for their work. Too many teachers feel they have no autonomy in their work because they enslave themselves to externalism. In their need for recognition, they inevitably get demolished by anti-recognition.

The affirmation, after all, isn't about the kids — it's about us. It's us saying, “I've got this insatiable need for affirmation, and I need my students or my principal to fulfill it.” I'm dumbfounded by how many teachers fool themselves into thinking they love their students when actually they love the way their students make them feel.

And the final step is, instead of needing the affirmation, we need to want the results. I didn't teach Caleb hoping he'd one day call me (see the end of this post), but I certainly taught Caleb hoping his life would turn out well and that my English Language Arts class would help.

But it's exactly the opposite — I'm telling you that the only way to care enough is by detaching your self-worth; I'm saying that you don't really care, cleanly, until you've rid yourself of needing affirmation and filled yourself up with the drive to harvest the fruits that affirmation points to. That's where the truly courageous teachers live and do their work.
